lines.trans: If I'm going in, I want you to go in too.
It's a meeting on Monday morning!
But it's pointless for me to join that meeting.
They say a lot of things that I don't understand.
You're sweet. Let me tell you something.
Look in there. Do you see that young woman over there?
She's a fire warden.
She came here to check a fire extinguisher.
Now she's in a meeting with our team.
That slows everyone else down! I have a lot to sort out.

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Takes present subjunctive entre after querer que (eu quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
I want you to go in too.

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Adds another person or item to what was already stated.

examples.trans: I want you to go in too.
I'm the one who made it too!

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: A gathering of people for a purpose. Here a workplace meeting; the final diphthong is nasal.

examples.trans: I’m not going to the meeting.

meanings.note: First workday of the week in Portuguese, literally second fair counting from Sunday.

examples.text: É uma reunião segunda-feira de manhã!
examples.trans: It's a meeting on Monday morning!

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Part of the day before noon; de manhã means in the morning.

examples.trans: We have a meeting in the morning.
I work better in the morning.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Built from in- + útil (useful); same form for masculine and feminine.

examples.trans: It's pointless to join that meeting.

meanings.note: Construes with de in Brazil (participar dessa reunião).

examples.trans: It's pointless to join that meeting.
Are you going to join today?

meanings.note: Contraction of de + essa before a feminine singular noun, required after verbs like participar de.

examples.trans: I'm not going to join that meeting.

meanings.note: Third-person masculine or mixed-gender plural subject pronoun.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Very frequent general noun; singular muita coisa naturally translates as a lot of things.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Regular -er verb for grasping meaning or an explanation.

examples.trans: I don't understand any of this.

meanings.note: Affectionate word for cute or sweet, used teasingly here toward a naive coworker.
Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Informal singular object pronoun, routinely mixed with você in warm everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: Used as a quick imperative olha! (look!) and in future subjunctive se vocês olharem (if you look).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Full form of informal pra; introduces purpose before an infinitive or direction.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.

meanings.note: Indicates the interior of a room or space, often paired with lá or para.
Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Gerund vendo pairs with estar (tá vendo, do you see), and tem que ver means we have to look into it.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
We need to look into that later.

meanings.note: Points to someone or something further away from both speakers.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
That chart over there is great.

meanings.note: Polite everyday Brazilian word for a young woman.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?

meanings.note: Points to something visible a short distance away.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
The room is right over there.

meanings.note: Third-person feminine singular pronoun; in informal Brazilian speech olha pra ela uses ela after a preposition too.
Trained workplace fire-safety responder; same form for masculine and feminine.

examples.trans: The fire warden checked the room.

meanings.note: An accidental or destructive fire, distinct from fogo (general fire/flame).

examples.text: A porta de incêndio está livre.

meanings.note: Irregular verb: present ele vem (he comes), completed past ela veio (she came).

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Safety cylinder inspected in offices and corridors.

examples.trans: She came to check a fire extinguisher.
The extinguisher is on the wall.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Contraction of em + uma before a feminine singular noun.

examples.trans: I work on a good team.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: First-person plural possessive agreeing in gender and number with the noun.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Standard Brazilian spelling for a work team or crew.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Transitively delays other people (atrasa os outros) or intransitively runs late (a reunião atrasou).
Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Everyday workplace verb for handling tasks, errands, or problems.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.
I need to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
